# 🧠 What is Machine Learning?

## You already use ML every day 🌍

::: {.incremental}
- 🎵 **Spotify Wrapped** clusters songs into your "vibes" — *unsupervised learning*.
- 📸 **iPhone "People" album** auto-tags faces in your photos — *supervised classification*.
- 🎬 **Netflix recommendations** predict what you'll like next — *collaborative filtering*.
- 💳 **Apple Pay fraud detection** flags weird transactions in real-time — *anomaly detection*.
- 🤖 **ChatGPT** predicts the next word given everything you typed — *deep learning*.
- 🩺 **Apple Watch atrial fibrillation alerts** classify your heartbeat as normal vs. abnormal — *medical ML*.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Today you'll learn how the same toolkit applies to **YRBS** to predict youth risk behaviors. 💪
:::

---

## Vocabulary cheat sheet 📖

The 10 words you'll hear all week:

| Term | What it means |
|------|---------------|
| **Outcome** (target, label, y) | The variable you want to predict |
| **Predictor** (feature, x) | The variables you predict *from* |
| **Training set** | The data the model learns from |
| **Test set** | Held-out data for an honest performance check |
| **Validation set** | Data used during model development to tune |
| **Overfitting** | When the model memorizes train but flunks test |
| **Cross-validation** | A way to estimate test performance without touching the test set |
| **Hyperparameter** | A "knob" you set *before* training |
| **Bias** | Systematic error from too-simple models |
| **Variance** | Sensitivity to small changes in training data |

# 🌳 Types of Models

## Three reasons to build a model

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Descriptive
- Describe or visualize patterns in data.
- No prediction, no inference — just understanding.
- Example: a **boxplot of BMI by sex**.

### Inferential
- Test a specific hypothesis about a **population**.
- Produces estimates, confidence intervals, p-values.
- Example: *"does this drug prolong life?"* → clinical trial → t-test.

### Predictive
- Make the **most accurate prediction** possible for new data.
- Often trades interpretability for accuracy.
- Example: *"will this patient be re-admitted within 30 days?"* → ML model.

:::

::: {.footer}
[Tidy Modeling With R](https://www.tmwr.org/software-modeling.html)
:::

# 🏷️ Supervised vs Unsupervised

## The big split

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Supervised 👨‍🏫
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
**You have an outcome (`y`). The model learns the mapping `x → y`.**

Two flavors:

- **Classification** — predict a *category* (Yes/No, A/B/C).
  *Did the student carry a weapon to school?*
- **Regression** — predict a *number*.
  *How many hours of sleep does the student get?*

Popular algorithms: logistic regression, decision trees, random forest, KNN, XGBoost.
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/supervised.png){width="80%"}
:::
:::

### Unsupervised 🕵️
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
**No outcome — the model finds *structure* in the data on its own.**

Two flavors:

- **Clustering** — group similar observations.
  *Are there "types" of high-school students?*
- **Dimensionality reduction** — compress many variables into a few summary axes.
  *PCA, UMAP.*

Popular algorithms: k-means, hierarchical clustering, PCA, t-SNE.
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/unsupervised.png){width="80%"}
:::
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 This week we focus on **supervised classification** — predicting Yes/No outcomes from YRBS.
:::

# 📐 Statistics + Machine Learning

## Different goals, same toolkit

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Statistical inference 🧪**

- Question: *"What does this tell us about the population?"*
- Focus: estimate **β**, get CIs, run hypothesis tests.

$${y} = \alpha + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \beta_nx_n + \epsilon$$

Care about: **interpretability**, uncertainty.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Machine learning 🤖**

- Question: *"What's my best guess for *this* observation's `y`?"*
- Focus: estimate **ŷ** as accurately as possible.

$$\hat{y} = \hat{f}(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$$

Care about: **predictive accuracy** on new data.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## They overlap more than people admit
- A logistic regression is *both*: you can interpret βs **and** use it to predict.
- Modern researchers fluently switch between the two perspectives.
- Don't pick a side — pick the right tool for your question.
:::
:::

::: {.footer}
[Introduction to Statistical Learning](https://www.statlearning.com/)
:::

# 😈 The 3 Cardinal Sins of ML

## Sin #1 — Overfitting

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- The model **memorized** the training data instead of learning the *pattern*.
- Performance is great on the data it saw, **terrible** on new data.
- Like a student who memorizes practice answers but can't solve a new problem.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## How to detect it
**Train accuracy = 99%, test accuracy = 60%.** That gap is overfitting screaming at you.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/bias-variance.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

---

## Sin #2 — Data leakage 🚰

::: {.incremental}
- **Information from the test set "leaked"** into model training.
- Your test metrics become a lie — they're inflated.
- **Examples of leakage:**
  - You imputed missing values using the **whole** dataset before splitting.
  - You normalized predictors using the **whole** dataset's mean.
  - You did feature selection using the **whole** dataset's correlations.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## How `tidymodels` protects you
When your `recipe` lives inside a `workflow()`, all preprocessing is **learned only from the training data** at each fold. No leakage. 🛡️
:::
:::

---

## Sin #3 — Class imbalance ⚖️

::: {.incremental}
- One outcome class is much more common than the other.
- Example: in YRBS only **~8%** of students report carrying a weapon to school.
- **A model that always predicts "No" gets 92% accuracy** — and is *useless*.
- That's why you need to look at **sensitivity, specificity, and ROC AUC**, not just accuracy.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## What to do about it
- ✅ **Stratify** your splits and folds (`strata = outcome`).
- ✅ **Downsample** the majority class with `step_downsample()` from `themis`.
- ✅ Use **ROC AUC**, not accuracy, as your tuning metric.
:::
:::

# 🔪 How Do We Spend Our Data?

## Always split first

![](https://media.tenor.com/EWRvErYGzPUAAAAM/bugs-bunny-looney-tunes.gif){fig-align="center" width="40%"}

::: {.incremental}
1. The **training set** is used to estimate model parameters.
2. The **test set** is used for an **independent** assessment of performance.
3. 🚫 The test set is **sacred**: do not peek during training.
:::

::: {.footer}
[Machine Learning with Tidymodels](https://workshops.tidymodels.org/)
:::

---

## Train / Validation / Test 🧪

![](img/validation.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.incremental}
- **Training set** — fit the model parameters.
- **Validation set** — pick the best hyperparameters / compare candidates.
- **Test set** — final, honest evaluation. Look once. Done.
:::

# 🔁 Resampling Methods

## What is resampling?

A way to estimate model performance **without touching the test set** — by repeatedly drawing samples from the training data.

![](img/rsamples.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

::: {.footer}
[`rsample` package](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/reference/index.html)
:::

---

## V-fold cross-validation 🥧

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
1. Split the **training** set into **K** folds (usually 5 or 10).
2. Train on K−1 folds, evaluate on the held-out fold.
3. Repeat K times. Average the results.

> Each row of the training data acts as both training *and* validation — but never both at the same time.
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/cv.png)
:::
:::

::: {.footer}
[K-Fold vs. Leave-One-Out](https://www.baeldung.com/cs/cross-validation-k-fold-loo)
:::

---

## Leave-One-Out CV 🎯

![](img/loocv.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

- Each observation gets its own fold.
- **Use when**: you have very little data (< 100 rows).
- **Avoid when**: you have lots of data (it's *very* slow — 12,000 folds for 12,000 rows!).

---

## Bootstrapping 🪣

![](img/boostrap.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

- Sample **with replacement** from the training set.
- Each bootstrap sample is the same size as the original — but some rows appear multiple times.
- **Use when**: small datasets where you want robust estimates.

---

## When do I use which?

| Method | Best for | Compute time ⏱️ |
|--------|----------|----------------|
| **5- or 10-fold CV** | Default for almost everything | 💚 Fast — fits 5–10 models |
| **Bootstrap** | Small datasets, uncertainty estimates | 💛 Medium — usually 25–100 models |
| **Leave-One-Out** | Tiny datasets (< 100 rows) | 🔴 Slow — fits **N** models (one per row!) |

::: {.callout-note}
## What does "compute time" mean?
Each method **trains your model multiple times** to estimate its performance honestly. The more models it trains, the longer your laptop has to spin its fan. 🔥

For 12,000 YRBS rows: 5-fold CV ≈ a few seconds. LOO ≈ 12,000 fits ≈ ☕☕☕.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 **For your YRBS project**: 5-fold CV with `strata = outcome`. Done. ✅
:::

# ⚖️ Bias–Variance Trade-off

## The core tension of ML

::: {.incremental}
- **Bias** — error from a model that's **too simple** to capture the truth.
- **Variance** — error from a model that's **too sensitive** to small changes in training data.
- Reduce one and you usually increase the other.
- The art of ML is finding the **sweet spot**.
:::

::: {.footer}
[Fortman-Roe, 2012](http://scott.fortmann-roe.com/docs/BiasVariance.html)
:::

---

## Two ends of the spectrum 🎯

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**High bias 🪨** ("underfit")

- Always predicts "No" → 92% accuracy on YRBS but useless.
- A linear model trying to fit a curved relationship.
- ✅ **Stable** across different training sets
- ❌ **Wrong** systematically
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**High variance 🎢** ("overfit")

- A decision tree that grows until each leaf is one row.
- Perfect on train, terrible on test.
- ✅ **Flexible** enough for any pattern
- ❌ **Unstable** — small data changes → very different model
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## The sweet spot
**Just complex enough to capture the real pattern, simple enough to generalize.**
We find this by tuning hyperparameters on resamples.
:::
:::

---

## The bullseye view 🎯

![](img/bullseye.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

::: {.footer}
[Fortman-Roe, 2012](http://scott.fortmann-roe.com/docs/BiasVariance.html)

# 🎛️ Hyperparameters

## What is a hyperparameter?

::: {.incremental}
- A **parameter** is something the model *learns* from data (like a regression coefficient β).
- A **hyperparameter** is a knob *you* set **before** training.
- Different hyperparameter values → very different models.
- We pick the best ones using **resampling + tuning**.
:::

---

## One example per algorithm

| Algorithm | Key hyperparameter | What it controls |
|-----------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Lasso / Ridge** | `penalty` | How aggressive the regularization is |
| **K-Nearest Neighbors** | `neighbors` | How many neighbors vote |
| **Decision Tree** | `tree_depth` | How deep the tree can grow |
| **Random Forest** | `mtry`, `trees` | Predictors per split, # of trees |
| **XGBoost** | `learn_rate`, `trees` | Step size + # of boosting rounds |

::: {.fragment}
> 🚀 **Tomorrow** you'll see `tune()` placeholders in your spec — that tells `tidymodels` *"try a grid of values for this knob and pick the best one."*
:::

# 🧭 The Full ML Process

## Step by step

::: {.incremental}
1. **Collect** data.
2. **Explore** + clean (you did this Tuesday).
3. **Split** — train / test.
4. **Recipe** — preprocessing.
5. **Spec** — choose a model.
6. **Workflow** — bundle them.
7. **Tune** hyperparameters with resamples.
8. **Fit** the final model on all training data.
9. **Evaluate** on the test set — *once*.
10. **Communicate** — render your website + share the link. 🌐
:::
